hypotheses.justification:
The current proof needs `[QuasiCompact f]` only to rewrite with `Scheme.Hom.ker_apply`, which says `f.ker.ideal U = RingHom.ker (f.app U).hom`. The equation itself holds without it. In Mathlib, `f.ker` is defined as `ofIdeals fun U ↦ RingHom.ker (f.app U).hom` (IdealSheaf/Basic.lean:691). That is the largest ideal sheaf whose ideals are contained in these kernels, and it does not depend on quasi-compactness.

Proof without the instance: `le_antisymm _ (le_radical _)`.
- `f.ker ≤ f.ker.radical` is `IdealSheafData.le_radical`.
- For `f.ker.radical ≤ f.ker`, unfold `Hom.ker` and use `le_ofIdeals_iff` (`I ≤ ofIdeals J ↔ I.ideal ≤ J`). It is then enough to show, for every affine open `U`, that `(f.ker.ideal U).radical ≤ RingHom.ker (f.app U).hom` (using `radical_ideal`).
- `Hom.ideal_ker_le` (no quasi-compactness) gives `f.ker.ideal U ≤ RingHom.ker (f.app U).hom`. `Ideal.radical_mono` turns this into `(f.ker.ideal U).radical ≤ (RingHom.ker (f.app U).hom).radical`.
- That kernel is radical: it equals `⊥.comap (f.app U).hom`, and `⊥` is radical because `Γ(X, f ⁻¹ᵁ U)` is reduced (from `[IsReduced X]`). This is the same `Ideal.isRadical_bot.comap` step as in the original proof.

This matches the geometric fact that the scheme-theoretic image of a reduced scheme is reduced for any morphism, quasi-compact or not. The instance is not used anywhere else in the statement.
